body.en: Beyond quadratics lie cubics, quartics and higher. Two questions dominate: where are the zeros, and what does the graph do at its ends? The leading term answers the second on its own.

label.en: ▲ Reference — End behaviour & the factor theorem

body.en: The end behaviour of a polynomial is governed entirely by its leading term \( a x^{n} \): the sign of \( a \) and the parity of \( n \). And \( (x-r) \) is a factor exactly when \( r \) is a zero (\( f(r)=0 \)).

Structural Decomposition Theorem: Any proper rational expression \(\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) with \(\deg P < \deg Q\) over \(\mathbb{R}\) decomposes uniquely into a sum of simpler fractions determined by the factorization of \(Q(x)\). When \(\deg P \ge \deg Q\), Euclidean polynomial division yields \(\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = Q_{\text{quot}}(x) + \dfrac{R(x)}{Q(x)}\) with \(\deg R < \deg Q\).

For distinct linear factors \((x - a_1)(x - a_2)\), Heaviside's cover-up rule gives the exact residue \(A_k = \lim_{x \to a_k} (x - a_k)\dfrac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\). For a repeated factor \((x - a)^m\), all intermediate powers \((x - a)^1, (x - a)^2, \dots, (x - a)^m\) must be included to span the full \(m\)-dimensional rational subspace.

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Polynomial Functions)

body.en:
Why Heaviside Cover-Up & Repeated-Factor Forms Work: Consider \(\dfrac{px + q}{(x - 5)(x + 4)} \equiv \dfrac{A}{x - 5} + \dfrac{B}{x + 4}\). Multiplying both sides by \((x - 5)(x + 4)\) yields the polynomial identity:

\[ px + q \equiv A(x + 4) + B(x - 5) \]

Because two polynomials equal on \(\mathbb{R} \setminus \{5, -4\}\) must be equal for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) by continuity, setting \(x = 5\) annihilates the \(B\) term and isolates \(A = \dfrac{5p + q}{9}\). For a repeated root \((x - a)^2\), writing only \(\dfrac{B}{(x - a)^2}\) restricts the numerator to a constant \(B\), which cannot match a general linear numerator \(px + q\); adding \(\dfrac{A}{x - a}\) supplies \(A(x - a) + B\), spanning all degree-1 numerators.

Find the zeros of \( f(x)=x^{3}-9x \).

Factor out \( x \), then a difference of squares:

\[ x(x^{2}-9)=x(x-3)(x+3)=0 \ \Rightarrow\ x=0,\ 3,\ -3. \]

Find the remainder when \( x^{2}+3x-4 \) is divided by \( (x-1) \).

By the remainder theorem, evaluate at \( x=1 \):

\[ 1+3-4=0. \]

body.en:
• Remainder Theorem Evaluation Sign: When dividing by \((x - c)\), the remainder is \(f(c)\). Notice the sign flip: dividing by \((x + 3)\) requires evaluating \(f(-3)\), not \(f(3)\).
  • Root Multiplicity and Axis Crossing: A root with odd multiplicity (e.g. 1, 3) crosses the \(x\)-axis; a root with even multiplicity (e.g. 2, 4) is tangent to the axis (touches and rebounds without crossing).
  • Missing Degree Terms in Long/Synthetic Division: Always check that exponents decrease consecutively: \(x^4, x^3, x^2, x^1, x^0\). If a term is missing (e.g. \(x^3 - 7x + 6\)), you must insert a \(0x^2\) placeholder in the division tableau.
  • Rational Root Theorem List: All possible rational zeros must have the form \(\pm p/q\), where \(p\) divides the constant term \(a_0\) and \(q\) divides the leading coefficient \(a_n\). Never invert this ratio!

Step-by-Step Solution: Applying Polynomial Functions principles, \(8-8+1=1\). Therefore, the verified correct option is \(1\).

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Polynomial Functions)

rows.en: Right-hand side has degree \(-1\) as \(x \to \infty\), whereas LHS approaches \(1\).
Two identical denominators merge into a single fraction, leaving an underdetermined system.
Include every power up to multiplicity: \(\tfrac{A}{x-5} + \tfrac{B}{(x-5)^2}\).
Using \(\tfrac{B}{x^2+4}\) for an irreducible quadratic factor
Fails to account for the \(x\)-term remainder when dividing by a degree-2 factor.
Always use a degree-1 numerator: \(\tfrac{Bx + C}{x^2 + 4}\).

question.en: Find all real and complex roots of the polynomial \(P(x) = 2x^3 + 3x^2 - 8x + 3\).

solution.en:
By the Rational Root Theorem, possible rational roots are \(\pm\{1, 3\}/\{1, 2\} = \pm\{1, 3, 1/2, 3/2\}\).

Test \(x = 1\): \[P(1) = 2(1)^3 + 3(1)^2 - 8(1) + 3 = 2 + 3 - 8 + 3 = 0. \quad \checkmark\]

So \((x - 1)\) is a factor. Divide \(P(x)\) by \((x - 1)\) using synthetic division:

\[2x^3 + 3x^2 - 8x + 3 = (x - 1)(2x^2 + 5x - 3).\]

Factor the remaining quadratic:

\[2x^2 + 5x - 3 = (2x - 1)(x + 3).\]

Setting each factor to zero yields the complete set of roots: \[x = 1, \quad x = \frac{1}{2}, \quad x = -3.\]
